papers.title: STWave: Fine-Scale Spatial Structure Discovery in Microscopic-Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics via Patchwise Wavelet Graphs.
papers.summary: STWave is a computational method designed to analyze microscopic-resolution spatial transcriptomics data, which captures gene expression at very fine spatial detail within tissue. It uses a patchwise wavelet graph approach to detect fine-scale spatial structures, essentially breaking the tissue into small patches and applying wavelet transforms on graph representations to reveal local patterns. This allows researchers to uncover subtle spatial organization of gene expression that might be missed by standard clustering or lower-resolution methods.
papers.why: This tool could help resolve fine-grained spatial gene expression patterns around interneurons and perineuronal nets in spatial transcriptomics datasets relevant to the PhD's neuronal autophagy research.
papers.figure: A figure showing STWave's detected fine-scale spatial domains overlaid on tissue compared to ground truth or alternative methods, ideally in a brain section example.

papers.title: A Practical Workflow for Spatial Transcriptomics Data Analysis: From Data Acquisition to Advanced Analyses.
papers.summary: This paper presents a practical, step-by-step workflow for analyzing spatial transcriptomics data, covering everything from initial data acquisition to more advanced downstream analyses. It likely walks through key stages such as quality control, normalization, clustering, spatial domain detection, and possibly cell-type deconvolution or trajectory analysis. The goal is to give researchers a clear, reproducible pipeline for handling spatial transcriptomics datasets in practice.
papers.why: A structured spatial transcriptomics workflow is directly useful for integrating spatial gene expression data with mitophagy/autophagy and interneuron studies in the brain, helping standardize analysis pipelines for the PhD project.

papers.title: CLEAR-ST: Physics-informed probabilistic decontamination of spatial transcriptomics by modeling mRNA lateral diffusion
papers.summary: CLEAR-ST is a new computational method that cleans up spatial transcriptomics data by explicitly modeling how mRNA molecules physically diffuse sideways between tissue spots, which otherwise causes signal contamination. It uses a physics-informed probabilistic framework to distinguish true gene expression signals from this diffusion-based noise, improving the accuracy of spatial gene expression maps. This approach could sharpen the resolution and reliability of spatial transcriptomic datasets, especially in tissues with fine cellular architecture like the brain.
papers.why: Cleaner spatial transcriptomics data is essential for accurately mapping gene expression around interneurons and perineuronal nets, where mRNA diffusion artifacts could otherwise obscure subtle cell-type-specific signals relevant to mitophagy and autophagy studies.
papers.figure: A figure showing before-and-after spatial gene expression maps demonstrating reduced diffusion-based signal bleed across tissue spots.

papers.title: Phenotype-associated spatial biomarker discovery in spatial transcriptomics with spHOT
papers.summary: This paper introduces spHOT, a computational method designed to discover spatial biomarkers in spatial transcriptomics data that are associated with specific phenotypes. It likely uses statistical or optimal transport-based techniques to link gene expression patterns across tissue space to biological or clinical outcomes. The tool aims to help researchers pinpoint genes whose spatial distribution correlates with disease states or cellular phenotypes.
papers.why: This method could help identify spatially resolved gene markers linked to neuronal phenotypes, such as interneuron subtypes or perineuronal net-associated states, within spatial transcriptomics datasets relevant to the mitophagy/autophagy project.

papers.title: Fzd7 Restrains Pink1-Dependent Mitophagy in Suture Stem Cells to Maintain Cranial Suture Patency.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the Wnt receptor Fzd7 regulates suture stem cells in the skull, which maintain the open, flexible joints (sutures) between skull bones during growth. The researchers found that Fzd7 acts to suppress Pink1-driven mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria, in these stem cells. When this restraint is lost, excessive mitophagy disrupts suture stem cell function, leading to premature fusion of the sutures instead of keeping them open (patent).
papers.why: While focused on skull stem cells rather than neurons, this paper offers a useful mechanistic parallel for Pink1-dependent mitophagy regulation that could inform understanding of mitophagy control pathways relevant to neuronal and glial mitochondrial quality control in the brain.
papers.figure: Figure showing suture morphology and mitophagy markers (e.g., Pink1, LC3) in Fzd7-deficient versus control suture stem cells.

papers.title: PGAM5-mediated VDAC1 oligomerization facilitates ponatinib-induced cardiotoxicity via disrupting the mitophagy-mitochondrial unfolded protein response synergistic defense crosstalk.
papers.summary: This study looks at how the cancer drug ponatinib damages heart cells by affecting mitochondria. It finds that a protein called PGAM5 causes another protein, VDAC1, to clump together on mitochondria, which disrupts two protective cellular processes: mitophagy (clearing damaged mitochondria) and the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (a stress-repair system). When these two defense systems fail to work together properly, heart cells become more vulnerable to damage from the drug.
papers.why: This paper offers useful mechanistic insight into how disruption of the mitophagy pathway and its crosstalk with mitochondrial stress responses can drive cell damage, which is conceptually relevant to studying mitophagy dysregulation in neurons.

papers.title: Astaxanthin alleviates dibutyl phthalate-induced cardiotoxicity in zebrafish larvae by regulating mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study looks at zebrafish larvae exposed to dibutyl phthalate, a chemical known to harm heart tissue. The researchers found that astaxanthin, an antioxidant compound, could protect the heart by regulating mitophagy, the process cells use to clear damaged mitochondria. The findings suggest astaxanthin restores healthy mitochondrial turnover, reducing the cardiotoxic effects of the chemical.
papers.why: This paper offers insight into mitophagy regulation mechanisms that could inform how similar pathways are studied in neurons, even though the model system and organ differ from the brain focus of this PhD project.

papers.title: EGCG targeting autophagy in cardiovascular diseases: mechanisms and therapeutic potential.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how EGCG, a green tea polyphenol, influences autophagy pathways in the context of cardiovascular disease. It discusses molecular mechanisms by which EGCG modulates autophagic flux, including effects on mTOR, AMPK, and related signaling. The review also highlights EGCG's therapeutic potential for conditions like cardiac hypertrophy, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and atherosclerosis.
papers.why: While focused on cardiovascular tissue rather than brain, this review may offer transferable insights into autophagy pathway regulation relevant to mitophagy mechanisms being studied in neurons.
